title: The Quiet Interior
premise: Lena Sandoval has spent seven years working the night shift at the Meridian Library, cataloguing other people's lives while leaving her own unspoken — above all her love for Tomas, the building's aging caretaker, whom she has never once told how she feels. When a box of undelivered letters from 1968 surfaces behind a wardrobe during renovations, she discovers they were written by her grandmother to a man Lena's family erased, and that Tomas knew him. As the letters pull her into her family's buried history of duty over desire, Tomas receives a diagnosis that gives their almost-saying-it an expiration date. In the end, Lena reads the final letter aloud in the library at dawn — saying goodbye properly to the grandmother she never met and, finally out loud, telling Tomas everything before his time runs out.
about_author: N. M. Okonkwo is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing private correspondence collections in Lagos and Lisbon before turning to fiction. They write quietly devastating stories about the things families refuse to say and the strangers who end up saying them.

chapters.title: The Hours Between
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A night shift at the Meridian Library: shelving returned books, watching insomniacs read, exchanging wordless rituals with Tomas the caretaker. Establishes the city that sleeps less every year and the seven years of things unsaid. Emotional beat: tenderness disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A near-confession on the loading dock interrupted by a fire alarm; Tomas walks her home through rain without either of them speaking. Flashback fragments to the night seven years ago when she first decided not to say it. Beat: the ache of practiced restraint.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Renovation crews open a sealed cavity behind a second-floor wardrobe and find a tin box: forty-one letters, all addressed to 'E.' and never delivered, dated 1968–1970. The handwriting stops her cold — it is her grandmother's. Beat: the past arriving like weather.

chapters.title: E.
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, intercut with the first letter. She learns 'E' was Emeka, a Nigerian student her grandmother loved before marrying the respectable man Lena descends from. The library's records show Emeka donated books here once. Beat: inheritance as a locked room.

chapters.title: The Man Who Swept the Floors
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV for the first time. He recognizes the name Emeka immediately — they were friends in 1968 — and decides not to tell Lena yet, protecting her from a story he thinks will only wound her. Beat: kindness that becomes concealment.

chapters.title: Reading Someone Else's Mail
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Alone in the stacks at 3 a.m., she reads letter after letter, mapping her grandmother's voice onto her own life. Her mother calls with mundane news; Lena cannot bring herself to mention the box. Beat: complicity beginning.

chapters.title: What Duty Built
chapters.summary: Lena visits her mother, Adaeze, probing gently about Grandma Ruth's youth. Adaeze reveals only that Ruth 'made the right choice,' and that the family paid a price for it no one names. Beat: the architecture of silence across generations.

chapters.title: The Undelivered
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She tracks down Emeka's last known address and finds he died two years ago — but lived four blocks from the library for decades. The undelivered letters were, impossibly, nearly delivered after all. Beat: grief for a parallel life.

chapters.title: A Cough in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. His diagnosis lands: pulmonary fibrosis, months not years. He keeps working nights because the library is where his life happened. He watches Lena carry the box and knows his secret-keeping now has a deadline too. Beat: mortality entering quietly.

chapters.title: Letter Nineteen
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Letter nineteen describes Ruth standing outside Emeka's boarding house, unable to knock — the exact scene of Lena's own interrupted confession on the loading dock. She begins to understand she has been rehearsing her grandmother's life. Beat: recognition, vertigo.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Tomas finally tells Lena about Emeka: the friendship, the deportation threat, the promise to deliver the letters that he failed to keep. Lena's anger and gratitude collide. Beat: the truth as both wound and gift.

chapters.title: Adaeze's Door
chapters.summary: Lena confronts her mother with the letters. Adaeze breaks: she found one letter as a girl, was made to burn it, and has hated the family's silence ever since. Mother and daughter grieve together for the first time. Beat: inherited shame cracking open.

chapters.title: Nights Getting Shorter
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. His breathing worsens; he starts writing something in a notebook he hides in his coat. Lena notices but doesn't ask. Their rituals deepen — tea at 2 a.m., shared silences — now charged with countdown. Beat: love sharpened by scarcity.

chapters.title: The Last Address
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She finds Emeka's daughter, Grace, running a small bookshop. Grace never knew about Ruth. Lena must decide whether delivering forty-year-old letters heals or merely disturbs. Beat: the ethics of honesty.

chapters.title: Grace
chapters.summary: Grace's POV. Reading her father's kept photograph of Ruth, Grace realizes her father's lifelong bachelorhood was an answer to a question no one asked him. She asks Lena to read her one letter aloud. Beat: strangers bound by other people's courage.

chapters.title: What the Letters Cost
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She reconstructs why the letters were hidden: Ruth's husband found them, and hiding them — not burning them — was his one act of mercy. Lena sees her grandfather whole for the first time. Beat: compassion complicating anger.

chapters.title: The Notebook
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Tomas collapses in the stacks; hospital tests confirm the decline. In his coat she finds the notebook — decades of unsent notes addressed to her, one per year, mirroring the box. Beat: devastation and recognition entwined.

chapters.title: Saying It
chapters.summary: Hospital room, dual POV. Lena says it — plainly, out loud, seven years late. Tomas confesses he stayed silent believing he was sparing her a caretaker's deathbed. They forgive each other for the years the silence cost. Beat: the climax of speech against duty.

chapters.title: Deliveries
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She delivers the letters to Grace, reads the final one aloud in the bookshop — Ruth's goodbye, written the week she married. Grace gives Lena Emeka's reply draft, never sent, saying he understood. Beat: goodbye performed properly at last.

chapters.title: Dawn Shift
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Home from hospital, Tomas asks for one night back at the library. At dawn they open the doors early and let the sleepless city in, together, his hand in hers. Beat: grace inside diminishment.

chapters.title: The Quiet Interior
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Tomas dies in October, held and told, everything said. Lena donates the letters and notebook to the library's archive under a joint label: Sandoval / Okonkwo Collection. Beat: mourning without regret.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, one year later. She leads the library's new midnight reading hour for the sleepless, opening each session by reading one archived letter aloud. On the anniversary she reads her own — the one she wrote to Tomas and finally mailed to nowhere. Beat: resolution; silence broken, permanently.
